name: Refrigerant leak detectors
summary: A handheld wand that sniffs for refrigerant escaping from fridge, freezer, heat-pump and air-conditioning lines, beeping faster as the tip nears the leak.
uses: Finds small leaks at joints and coils: down to about 1 to 3 g a year on good units (FIELDPIECE DRX3, FIELDPIECE SRL2)
Some aren't made for ammonia (R-717) or CO2 (R-744) systems, so check the label before trusting a quiet wand there (FIELDPIECE DRX3)
Not every model sees flammable R-290 or R-600a: some list only CFC, HCFC and HFC, so check the label (FIELDPIECE SRL2, FIELDPIECE DRX3)
Leak finders only: Fieldpiece says the DRX3 is not a safety device for monitoring refrigerant or heating-gas levels (FIELDPIECE DRX3)
Wind, draughts and one big leak can hide small ones (ACHR LEAKS)
A leak finder reads refrigerant, not oxygen; R-22's safety card says a leak can lower the oxygen in a closed room (INCHEM ICSC 0049), and a monitor with an O2 sensor can alarm below 19.5% (MSA 4XR)
identify: A handheld wand with a flexible probe and a sensor tip or filter at the end (FIELDPIECE DRX3, FIELDPIECE SRL2); Fieldpiece and Uniweld make the models cited here. Electronic kinds (FIELDPIECE SRL2, ACHR LEAKS): heated diode, which reads the absolute level and can be held on a leak and keep beeping, and is very sensitive when new, but loses sensitivity with use and needs new tips (the DRX3 starts in auto-zero, which resets every 3 seconds, so keep its tip moving at about 7.6 cm (3 in) a second; manual zero holds the baseline); infrared, which pumps air past an IR cell and reacts only to a change, so the wand must keep moving at 2.5 to 7.5 cm (1 to 3 in) a second, keeps its sensitivity for about 10 years and dislikes knocks; and corona-suppression units, which ACHR says are less accurate and more prone to false triggering than heated-diode ones. Labels to look for: EN 14624, the refrigerant families it finds (CFC, HCFC, HFC, HFO, HC) and safety classes (A1, A2L, A3), sensitivity in g/yr or oz/yr, and for flammable refrigerants a Class I Division 2 or ATEX Zone 2 mark (FIELDPIECE DRX3, FIELDPIECE SRL2). A halide torch is a small propane torch with a sampling hose and a copper plate; its blue flame turns green at chlorine-bearing refrigerants (UNIWELD PLD33V). Don't use one: the R-22 safety card says flame contact makes toxic gas (INCHEM ICSC 0049).
test: Switch on in clean air and let it warm up and self-calibrate, about 30 seconds on an SRL2 (FIELDPIECE SRL2). Then give it a known leak, outdoors and away from ignition sources. Fieldpiece's DRX3 check: cap a refrigerant cylinder's port tightly, crack the valve to wet the inside of the cap, close it, remove the cap and wave the tip over it; at high sensitivity a good DRX3 goes near full scale, and if not, the sensor may need replacing (FIELDPIECE DRX3). Heated-diode tips last about 300 hours of use, and some meters count the hours (FIELDPIECE DRX3). Infrared units: check the filter; a wet one chokes the airflow and must be changed, and the unit must never run without one (FIELDPIECE SRL2). Batteries: an SRL2's lithium-ion pack loses about 30% of its run time after 500 charges or 2 years (FIELDPIECE SRL2); AA models need fresh cells. A unit that stays silent on a known leak may need a new sensor tip (FIELDPIECE DRX3) or a dry filter (FIELDPIECE SRL2): don't trust it. One that alarms everywhere may be in air already full of refrigerant: lower the sensitivity (FIELDPIECE SRL2). For flammable refrigerants use only a unit rated for them, and change its tip or batteries away from the leak (FIELDPIECE DRX3).

decay.note: Infrared cells keep working about 10 years, but their lithium-ion packs lose about 30% of run time in 2 years (FIELDPIECE SRL2); heated-diode tips wear out after about 300 hours of use (FIELDPIECE DRX3).

improvise: Soapy water brushed on joints shows bubbles at a leak; it's the oldest method, but it misses very small leaks and fails in wind (ACHR LEAKS). If the system already has UV dye in its oil, a UV or blue light shows a glow at the leak (ACHR LEAKS). Don't use a halide torch. Its open flame breaks refrigerant down into toxic gases, including phosgene, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen fluoride (INCHEM ICSC 0049, for R-22). It finds only chlorine-bearing CFC and HCFC refrigerants, not R-410A (UNIWELD PLD33V), and a flame near flammable refrigerants such as R-290 or R-600a, or near fuel gas, can start a fire or explosion (FIELDPIECE DRX3, RBQ GAS). UEi's CD100A combustible-gas sniffer also reacts to refrigerants, but gives only a tick rate, not which gas (UEI CD100A). None of these says whether the air is safe: breathing a lot of refrigerant vapour can starve the brain of oxygen (FIELDPIECE DRX3), and R-22's safety card says a leak can lower the oxygen in a closed room (INCHEM ICSC 0049). A leak finder reads refrigerant, not oxygen; a monitor with an O2 sensor can alarm below 19.5% (MSA 4XR). Work only in well-ventilated areas (FIELDPIECE DRX3); after a big leak in a small room, get out and air it out first: R-22's safety card warns of suffocation in confined areas (INCHEM ICSC 0049).
